```{r}
#| label: setup
library(hammel)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

A population can carry several categorical group dimensions at once, such as race and region. Each dimension is a column of the persons table, declared with `set_groups()`, and each has its own categories, inheritance rule, optional ancestry tracking and transitions. Rate tables, weight models, matching models and the analysis functions refer to dimensions by name.

This article builds a small example with two dimensions:

- **race**, with categories A and B, inherited from a random parent; and
- **region**, with categories North and South, inherited from the mother, with migration between regions.

The rates are simple illustrative values chosen so that each mechanism is easy to see. They are not demographic estimates.

## Starting population

`create_baseline_population()` can draw several dimensions. A named list of weights draws each dimension independently; a data frame with one column per dimension and a `weight` column gives their joint distribution. Here race and region are associated: B is more common in the South.

```{r}
#| label: baseline
set.seed(10)
start <- data.frame(
  race   = c("A", "B", "A", "B"),
  region = c("North", "North", "South", "South"),
  weight = c(0.45, 0.05, 0.30, 0.20)
)
pop <- create_baseline_population(20000, max_age = 70, groups = start)
count(pop$persons, race, region) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

## Declaring the dimensions

`set_groups()` declares every dimension with `group()`. Listing `categories` fixes their order: the first category is the reference level for group terms in weight and matching formulas. Each dimension has its own inheritance rule.

```{r}
#| label: declaration
model <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(pop) |>
  set_groups(
    race   = group(categories = c("A", "B")),
    region = group(categories = c("North", "South"), inheritance = "mother")
  )
```

## Rates by dimension

A rate table stratifies by the dimensions it has columns for, and dimensions without a column share the schedule. `stratify_rates()` adds proportional differences. Here mortality differs by region only and fertility by race only, so each process's cells are only as fine as its rates.

```{r}
#| label: rates
base_mortality <- data.frame(
  sex = rep(c("m", "f"), each = 3),
  age_start = rep(c(0, 1, 50), 2), age_end = rep(c(1, 50, Inf), 2),
  rate = rep(c(0.006, 0.0015, 0.045), 2)
)
mortality <- stratify_rates(base_mortality, list(region = c(North = 1, South = 1.3)))
fertility <- stratify_rates(data.frame(age_start = 15, age_end = 45, rate = 0.065),
                            list(race = c(A = 1, B = 1.25)))

model <- model |>
  set_mortality(mortality) |>
  set_fertility(fertility)
```

## Migration as a transition in one dimension

Group transitions are set per dimension with `set_group_transition(model, rates, group = ...)`, using `origin` and `destination` columns. A transition table may also be stratified by other dimensions: here people of race B move from North to South at twice the rate of race A.

```{r}
#| label: migration
migration <- data.frame(
  origin      = c("North", "North", "South", "South"),
  destination = c("South", "South", "North", "North"),
  race        = c("A", "B", "A", "B"),
  age_start = 18, age_end = 40,
  rate        = c(0.02, 0.04, 0.03, 0.03)
)
model <- set_group_transition(model, migration, group = "region")
```

Duration in a transition schedule counts from entering the current category of that dimension only, so moves in other dimensions do not reset it.

## Matching within one dimension

Matching group effects are named by dimension. Pair effects, restrictions and `delta` take a list keyed by dimension, and formula predictors are written `female_race`, `male_race` and `same_race`. For now, one dimension can carry matching effects (here race), and every matching model in a run must use the same one. Region has no matching effect, so partners' regions match only as often as availability makes them.

```{r}
#| label: matching
model <- set_union_formation(model, "on_demand",
  matching = create_age_gap_matching_model(2, 5,
    group_exogamy = list(race = c("A:B" = -2))),
  kinship_generations = 1)
```

## Weights by dimension

Weight models choose which member of a rate cell experiences an event, without changing the cell's rate. Their variables are named by dimension as well: `race`, `partner_region`, and for union processes `race_w`, `region_h` or `same_race`. Here unions dissolve at an overall rate, and dissolution falls more often on couples whose races differ.

```{r}
#| label: dissolution
model <- set_union_dissolution(model,
  data.frame(dur_start = 0, dur_end = Inf, rate = 0.02),
  weights = create_weight_model(~ same_race, c(same_race = log(0.5))))
```

## Simulating

```{r}
#| label: simulate
result <- simulate(model, 40, seed = 20)
```

The persons table has a column for each dimension, and the transition history names the dimension of each move.

```{r}
#| label: histories
result$persons |> select(person_id, sex, race, region) |> head()
result$transitions |> head()
count(result$transitions, group, origin, destination)
```

## Analysis by several dimensions

Every calculator's `by` accepts declared dimensions by name, several at once, with one column per dimension in the result.

```{r}
#| label: fig-population
#| fig-cap: Population by race and region over time
calculate_population_size(result, seq(0, 40, 5), by = c("race", "region")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = population, color = region, linetype = race)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "year", y = "population")
```

Rates recover the inputs, up to random variation. Mortality by region over ages 1 to 50 should be close to 0.0015 in the North and 0.00195 in the South, whatever the race:

```{r}
#| label: mortality
calculate_mortality_rates(result, c(0, 40), c(1, 50), by = c("region", "race")) |>
  filter(age_start == 1) |>
  select(sex, region, race, person_years, deaths, rate_mortality)
```

Migration rates are counted for one dimension, chosen with `group`, and can be split by the others. The age 18–40 rates should be close to the inputs above: 0.02 and 0.04 for moves to the South by race A and B, and 0.03 for moves to the North.

```{r}
#| label: transition-rates
calculate_transition_rates(result, c(0, 40), age_breaks = c(18, 40),
                           group = "region", by = "race") |>
  filter(age_start == 18) |>
  select(origin, destination, race, person_years, transitions, rate_transition)
```

Union rates split by each partner's categories, in any combination. `get_detailed_unions()` gives both partners' categories at the start of each union in every dimension:

```{r}
#| label: unions
get_detailed_unions(result) |>
  filter(start_time >= 0) |>
  count(race_w, race_h, region_w, region_h) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

Interracial unions are rare because of the race pair effect. Cross-region unions occur at the rate availability allows, since region has no matching effect.

Dissolution rates by whether the partners' races differ show the weight model: the overall rate is fixed by the input, but dissolutions fall more often on interracial unions.

```{r}
#| label: dissolution-rates
calculate_dissolution_rates(result, c(0, 40), c(0, Inf), by = c("race_w", "race_h")) |>
  select(race_w, race_h, union_years, dissolutions, rate_dissolution)
```

## Current limits

- Matching group effects use one dimension at a time. Joint calibration of matching across dimensions is planned; cross-dimension interactions, such as race exogamy that differs by region, are not available.
- Transition strata that a table does not cover have zero risk, unlike other rate tables, which must cover every category combination they use.
